sources_considered.why: Original survey provides contemporaneous reports of useful development applications. These are perceptions, not experimentally measured gains.
Original multinational evaluation measures errors in ordinary news responses.
Randomized experiment supplies material caution about coding benefits and self-reported productivity.
Positive field-experiment results were considered, but the summary does not establish that the experimental observations occurred in the selected 2025 period.
Relevant factuality research, but its deliberately selected hallucination prompts are less representative of ordinary use than the news evaluation.

evidence_items.locator: AI → AI Agents, Impacts of AI agents
evidence_items.explanation: Developer respondents report useful applications in their work, supporting the modest assertion that practical coding uses exist. Self-selection and subjective productivity estimates limit the strength of this evidence.

Responses generated in late May and early June across four assistants and multiple languages contained significant problems in 45% of cases. The report also records improvement in the comparable BBC subset, so persistent problems do not imply no progress.

In this experiment, experienced developers working on familiar repositories became slower despite believing AI helped. This limits reliance on perceived productivity and broad claims of coding gains, but does not negate the existence of some useful applications.

unresolved_gaps: These findings cannot establish that unreliability is unavoidable in every application or future architecture.
The evidence of current coding utility included here is self-reported; the experimental counterexample shows why reported time savings require caution.
